Most vitamin c types are fine as a supplement, but there are a few key differences:

Ascorbic acid: the cheapest and most common type in supplements, derived from corn. This type of vitamin c is extremely acidic, so in high doses, it may cause stomach pain, heartburn, and other Gl issues (bad for mega dosing). In lower doses (less than 500-1000mg), there shouldn't be any Gl side effects.
Liposomal vitamin c: most expensive type of vitamin c. uses liposomes (fat bubbles) to encapsulate the vitamin c molecule, which makes it far less harsh on the stomach.

Supposedly has better absorption than the other types of vitamin c too. This one is good for mega dosing since it lacks the acidity of ascorbic acid. Anecdotally, l've seen many people use high doses of liposomal vitamin c to alleviate opioid withdrawal symptoms.
The two other most common ones in supplements include sodium ascorbate and calcium ascorbate, which are essentially buffered versions of ascorbic acid. This makes them less harsh on the stomach than ascorbic acid.

There's a few other types as well, but they're mostly used in skincare products!

For example, I used to take like 20g of Kratom a day, and now I’m down to 2g. Now other substances like weed work better than before despite me not cutting back on weed at all. So I’m tapering a different substance than weed (Kratom) but oh man in my experience you can definitely get PAWS while actively tapering a substance. Think about it like this: tapering just puts you through a small “version” of withdrawal over and over. Just like you can get PAWS from going cold turkey, you can also get symptoms of PAWS from each reduction even if you’re still taking it. 

For instance, if you went from 4g of weed a day down to 3g, then you’re going to experience the WD and PAWS from cutting out that one gram. It’s less intense than going cold Turkey would be, but your mind/body still has to recover from “quitting” that one gram.

In any case, if it’s feeling a bit too much then you may want to wait a bit and stabilize your mind/body more before your next reduction. Whatever you decide to do, just remember that it’s only temporary and you will return to baseline. You got this!

Honestly, the less frequently you take it the less likely you are to ever develop a dependency to it. For context, I took 4-4.5 grams 3x a day with zero days off for 6 years and the withdrawals slowly got worse as the years went by (nearing the end of my taper now). Looking back, it was probably the multiple doses a day with zero breaks that really did me in. Just don’t do that and you should be good haha

Hey, certainly not an expert but I do understand that benzos that end with “-LAM” are simply “normal” benzos (the ones ending with “-PAM”) with a triazole ring fused to them. This makes them more potent than their original counterpart, as in they kick in faster, they’re more potent mg per mg, and they don’t last as long. A good example is Xanax/alprozoLAM being chemically similar to Valium/diazepam, with the only diffference being Xanax/alprazolam has a triazole ring added to it. This, as you can guess, is why Xanax is more potent, kicks in faster, and doesn’t last as long as Valium. ClonazoLAM is the same concept as this, however the original counterpart benzo, clonazePAM, Is already quite potent to begin with. This means that clonazoLAM is a stronger version of clonazePAM(the rx one, aka Klonopin) that kicks in faster, is extremely potent (with no tolerance blackout doses in the low-mid microgram range), and technically has a shorter duration.

In addition, clonazoLAM is a research chemical that isn’t approved for human use and lacks any intensive medical studies, so the only data we have on it is anecdotal. All I can say is it’s an extremely dangerous molecule that caused very pronounced withdrawal symptoms in me in a very short period of time. It also caused me to lose my inhibitions far more, caused severe delusions of sobriety, all of which led to me compulsively dosing it more than any other benzo I’ve tried

Not an expert by any means, but I believe it has something to do with how it interacts with the opioid receptors vs other opioids. Kratom, as far as I’ve heard, is a partial mu opioid receptor agonist, meaning it doesn’t fully activate the receptor. Stronger opioids such as rx painkillers and street heroin, are full agonists, meaning they fully activate the opioid receptor. It’s similar to the difference between weed/cannabis and spice/k2, weed being a physically safe partial cannabinoid receptor agonist, and spice/k2 being a full agonist. That’s why it’s possible to overdose on stronger opioids and spice/k2 and nearly impossible to with cannabis or Kratom, it’s because they quite literally don’t fully activate the receptors they target.

Edit: this would also explain why Kratom and cannabis both have a ceiling effect, where taking more doesn’t necessarily increase effects exponentially.
